messages.content: Identify all predictive claims made in August 2026 regarding short term BDI movements (30 day horizon), by conviction and consensus vs disagreement between analysts. Test these claims against September data.

August's consensus was near-term BDI firmness (Breakwave, Star Asia, Signal, Intermodal), with the explicit bearish outliers being Smart Shipbroking's forward-curve moderation call and the FIS FFA backwardation — and through 10 Sep the consensus has been vindicated (BDI +10.5% to 3,521, BCI +19.9% to 6,400), while neither bearish-forward call has materialized, though Smart Shipbroking's window runs to 18 Sep.

See the report for sources and charts.

highlights: ## Bi-Weekly Industry Report August 4, 2026

• Dry Bulk Rate Volatility Collapses as Spot Rates Remain High – The dry bulk market continues to trade at historically elevated levels with no immediate signs of a correction, while freight rate volatility has collapsed to multi-year lows. Current spot rate strength is primarily sustained by structural vessel supply constraints, driven by ongoing geopolitical disruptions and an intensive global drydocking schedule. However, downside risks are accumulating as weakening demand for iron ore in China, the sector's primary trading commodity, threatens to disrupt the market balance. Because freight rates are fundamentally demand-driven and supply enabled, the absence of sustained demand growth is gradually tilting the medium term outlook. While pinpointing the exact catalyst for a market correction remains challenging, investors should look past the current period of price stability, as macroeconomic fundamentals will ultimately drive medium-term freight dynamics. However, shipowners have been riding a very strong market for multiple years in a row and thus maintain extremely healthy cash balances to weather a potential storm, unlike the 2010’ crisis when major companies where forced to reorganize.

artifacts.title: BIMCO Dry Bulk Shipping Market Overview & Outlook - Cyprus Shipping News
artifacts.subtitle: Cyprusshippingnews

highlights: “Uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz remains central to the outlook. A three-week ceasefire between the US and Iran allowed transits to partly recover, but safety conditions have since deteriorated. Under normal market conditions, around 4% of dry bulk cargoes and tonne-mile demand sail through the strait,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO.

Given this uncertainty, BIMCO presents two forecast scenarios. The “SoH closed” scenario assumes that the strait remains effectively closed indefinitely, while the “SoH open” scenario assumes that it reopens by the end of the third quarter of 2026. The longer the closure persists, the closer the market outlook will resemble the SoH closed scenario.

A full return of dry bulk shipping to the Red Sea is not factored into either scenario, although a full return could lower tonne-mile demand by around two percent. The Houthis have announced a blockade of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports, increasing uncertainty over when commercial shipping may be able to fully return to the Red Sea.

artifacts.subtitle: gCaptain

highlights: Longer average sailing distances are expected to support dry bulk demand through 2026, helping offset rising fleet growth and keeping market conditions relatively stable before weakening in 2027, according to new analysis from BIMCO.

“We estimate that the dry bulk supply-demand balance will remain stable in 2026 and weaken in 2027,” said Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. “An improvement in the economic and demand outlook has led us to revise our 2026 demand forecast up by 0.5 percentage points.”

A key driver of dry bulk demand growth is the extension of average sailing distances, which BIMCO expects to increase by 0.5% to 1.5% annually through 2027. The shift is being driven primarily by rising iron ore and bauxite shipments from the South Atlantic to Asia, boosting tonne-mile demand even as overall cargo volumes face headwinds.

artifacts.title: Weekly Market Report
artifacts.subtitle: Broker PDF

highlights: The dry bulk rally gathered further pace, supported mainly by gains in the largest vessel classes. The BDI averaged 3,401 points, rising by 12% week on week. The Capesize segment continued to flourish, with C5TC earnings exceeding $58,000/day and reaching levels last seen in 2021. Prompt tonnage was absorbed as miners increased activity in the Pacific, while the Atlantic witnessed strong demand from South Brazil and West Africa. With demand holding firm across both basins, the market remains well supported, although it remains to be seen whether demand will sustain the momentum in the near term. Kamsarmax/Panamax rates strengthened as Australian and Indo nesian coal shipments supported Pacific employment, alongside additional cargoes divided into smaller parcels because of elevat ed Capesize rates. Owners remain optimistic about Australian mining exports. In the Atlantic, September demand sustained healthy fronthaul activity, although a possible slowdown in en quiry could allow available tonnage to build and weigh on rates in the near term, particularly if fresh cargo volumes fail to material ise. Ultramaxes/Supramaxes remained steady, with weighted aver age spot earnings fluctuating within a narrow range. Performance varied by region, with grain shipments from the Americas to Asia supporting selected routes and the US Gulf offering firmer condi tions. However, weaker Chinese steel demand continued to limit activity, while the Mediterranean remained sluggish amid weak cargo demand. The Handysize segment saw uneven performance last week, with rates edging higher. In the South Atlantic and US Gulf, sentiment firmed as rising cargo demand met balanced tonnage. Asian con ditions improved as enquiry increased, while subdued Mediterra nean activity limited overall gains. The outlook remains favoura ble in selected regions, although a broader advance will require a sustained improvement in cargo demand.

artifacts.title: August 2026 BDI predictions vs September outcomes
artifacts.subtitle: As of 2026-09-10 · history (Aug-2026 claims vs Sep-2026 data)

blocks.title: BDI and BCI daily, 16 Jun – 9 Sep 2026
blocks.subtitle: OilPriceAPI reprint of Baltic Exchange assessments

blocks.text: **Scope.** This is a retrospective test of predictive claims published in August 2026 with a ~30-day (September) horizon. The test window is partial: September data run through 10 Sep, and the one explicit numeric forecast (Smart Shipbroking) extends to 18 Sep. Most August commentary was retrospective or qualitative; the genuinely falsifiable 30-day claims are few. BDI = 40% BCI + 30% BPI + 30% BSI; the September move was Capesize-led.

rows.claim: No immediate signs of correction; spot strength held by structural supply constraints (geopolitics + drydocking). Medium-term downside risk accumulating on weak Chinese iron-ore demand.
Capesize FFA rallied; Sept contract $39,500/d vs spot C5TC $42,797/d — backwardation pricing in modest softening over 30 days. Options put/call <1 (bullish skew).

rows.src: BIMCO SMOO (Jul ed., operative in Aug) [3]
rows.claim: Supply/demand supportive in 2026, weakens 2027. SoH-open scenario (reopen by end-Q3) = comparatively stronger outlook.
Robust upward momentum from tightening fleet availability and Asian weather disruptions; Hormuz framework still cautious.
Prompt Capesize TCE $45,200/d but forward curve moderates to ~$33,900/d by 18 Sep; 'today's strength does not automatically roll into late September.'
Black Sea dry-bulk exports −42% vs spring; less cargo there but potentially more tonne-miles elsewhere if grain redirects to the Americas.
Demand-to-supply ratio 1.04 (demand growth slightly ahead of supply); C5TC in 88th percentile of trailing year.

blocks.title: Predictive claims made in August 2026 (30-day horizon)

blocks.text: **Consensus (5 of 7):** near-term BDI firmness — Breakwave ('no immediate correction'), Star Asia, Signal, Intermodal, and the physical market itself all pointed to continued support into September. **Disagreement:** the forward curve. Smart Shipbroking was the explicit bearish outlier (Capesize TCE −25% by 18 Sep); FIS FFA levels implied only mild softening; Breakwave flagged medium-term (not 30-day) downside on China iron ore. No August source predicted the magnitude of the September Capesize surge.
blocks.title: Consensus vs disagreement

rows.claim: FIS FFA: Sept contract $39,500/d implies softening [4]
rows.verdict: Not vindicated — spot ran far above the FFA-implied level

rows.claim: Smart Shipbroking: Capesize TCE moderates to ~$33,900 by 18 Sep [5]
rows.outcome: C5TC $54,791/d as of Wk36; no moderation through 10 Sep
rows.verdict: Not vindicated to date (window open to 18 Sep)

rows.claim: Star Asia / Signal / Intermodal: momentum holds [6][9][7]
rows.outcome: BDI +10.5%, BCI +19.9% vs 28 Aug; 7-session rally extended into Sep

rows.claim: Xclusiv: Black Sea slump, tonne-mile substitution [8]
rows.outcome: Black Sea wheat loadings −60% y/y in 5 wks to 28 Aug (Signal) [9]
rows.verdict: Driver confirmed; BDI impact offset by Capesize strength

blocks.text: 'Owners have good reason to defend current prompt levels, particularly in Capesize, but the forward curve argues against assuming today's strength automatically rolls into late September.'
blocks.attribution: Smart Shipbroking, Freight Market Outlook Week 35, 31 Aug 2026 [5]

blocks.text: **Caveats.** (1) The 30-day window is only ~one-third elapsed; Smart Shipbroking's moderation call is testable only through 18 Sep. (2) FFA levels are broker-reported market prices, not analyst forecasts — they embed expectations but are not a directional call by an analyst. (3) BIMCO's operative August vintage is the 30 July edition; no August SMOO edition was located. (4) BDI/BCI prints are OilPriceAPI reprints of Baltic Exchange assessments, not official Baltic data [1].

Markdown Content:
_By_[_Eirini Diamantara_](https://www.linkedin.com/in/eirini-diamantara-58b269105/)_&_[_Dimitris Roumeliotis_](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dimitris-roumeliotis-1364b224/)

The dry bulk freight market delivered a considerably stronger performance during the first seven months of 2026, with Baltic Exchange time-charter equivalent earnings improving across all four major vessel segments compared with January–July 2025. The recovery was broad-based rather than dependent on a single vessel class, reflecting stronger cargo volumes, improved fleet utilisation and firmer demand across both major and minor bulk trades.

Based on the available daily assessments, the Capesize 5TC averaged approximately USD 30,400/day, up 81% from USD 16,800/day during the corresponding period of 2025. Capesize earnings reached a high of USD 46,538/day in late May, while the market closed July at USD 35,457/day, well above the USD 26,858/day recorded at the end of July last year.The improvement extended across the smaller segments. Kamsarmax earnings averaged around USD 17,600/day, increasing 53% year-on-year from USD 11,500/day, while the Ultramax 11TC rose by 48% also near to USD 17,600/day. Handysize earnings recorded the smallest, but still substantial, increase, averaging USD 14,100/day compared with USD 10,100/day in 2025, representing growth of 39%. The progression of rates was also important.

Following a relatively stable opening quarter, earnings strengthened sharply during April and May, particularly for Capesizes and Kamsarmaxes. Ultramax and Handysize markets advanced more steadily, reaching their strongest levels during June and July and demonstrating healthier underlying support across geographically diversified trades. This stronger freight environment was accompanied by an increase in total seaborne dry bulk volumes. Based on the Signal Ocean data, approximately 3.41 billion tonnes were transported during January–July 2026, compared with 3.35 billion tonnes during the same period of 2025, representing growth of almost 2%. Capesize-carried cargo increased by 4.8% to 936.7 million tonnes, lifting its share of total trade from 26.7% to 27.4%. Panamax, Supramax and Handymax volumes also increased, while VLOC, Handysize and Small vessel cargoes declined. The figures therefore indicate that trade growth was concentrated mainly in the larger and medium-sized vessel categories, supporting the segments that experienced the strongest freight improvement.

Commodity flows remained dominated by iron ore and coal, which together represented more than 52% of total dry bulk trade. Iron ore volumes increased by 1.5% to 992.2 million tonnes, while coal shipments rose by 2.1% to 788.9 million tonnes. Grain trade delivered a more pronounced increase of 10.4%, reaching 358.9 million tonnes and overtaking other ores and rocks as the third-largest cargo category. By contrast, fertilizers, steel, cement and forestry products declined, confirming that overall growth was driven primarily by the traditional core commodities. Australia remained the largest origin, increasing exports to 844.8 million tonnes, followed by Brazil at 374.1 million tonnes. Guinea recorded one of the strongest increases, rising 22% to 131.9 million tonnes, supporting long-haul bauxite movements. China remained overwhelmingly the largest destination, receiving 1.36 billion tonnes, up 2.9% year-on-year and representing almost 40% of global dry bulk imports. South Korea, Vietnam and Indonesia also increased intake, while India declined by almost 5%.

Overall, the 2026 freight recovery appears firmly connected to improving physical trade. Higher iron ore, coal and grain volumes, combined with stronger long-haul exports from Australia, Brazil and Guinea, increased vessel employment and supported rates across the market. THE BALTIC Dry Index (BDI) ended last week at 3186 points for 28 August 2026, up from 21 August's figure of 2841.

## Capesize

The market maintained a broadly positive trajectory throughout the week, with the BCI 5TC building on its opening level and rising from $42,105 to $48,399, as Atlantic strength and a firmer Pacific combined to underpin sentiment. In the Pacific, initial gains were checked by a brief correction on Tuesday, but the market quickly regained momentum as sustained miner participation, together with operator-controlled cargoes, supported rates. The standout move came later in the week when C5 values surged above $16 for earlier arrivals, marking a significant recovery from the low $14s seen at the start of the week. The Atlantic provided the main catalyst for the week's advance. The North Atlantic firmed notably, with both transatlantic and front-haul routes posting healthy gains as fresh demand emerged and higher fixtures were concluded. South Brazil and West Africa to China business also strengthened early in the week, with C3 climbing into the high $37s. While momentum appeared to stall on Thursday amid limited bidding activity, underlying tonnage tightness continued to provide support. Owners remained firm with offers above $38, while charterers largely favoured older or larger vessels. Reports of $38.50 being fixed on more than one occasion emerged on Friday, however, injecting renewed confidence into the market and lifting sentiment heading into the weekend.

## Panamax-Kamsarmax

The market this week bounced back, with improvements everywhere. The North Atlantic went from minimal transatlantic enquiry to rates rising by almost $2,000 daily, with an 82,000-dwt fixed midweek at $20,500 delivery/redelivery Gibraltar via North Coast South America. Fronthaul in the North was already faring better, but also increased, with an 82,000-dwt open Liverpool fixed via the US Gulf to China at $32,750 at the start of the week (equivalent to low $29,000s BKI) which improved by around $1,000 daily by the weekend. East Coast South America was very active for second half September dates and the P6 gained about $2,000 daily during the week with an 80,000-dwt fixed basis Singapore at $22,000 in the middle of the week. Despite the Atlantic making most of the headlines, rates in Asia for round voyages saw the biggest increases driven by North Pacific grains and Australian mineral demand, added to the improving East Coast South American market. At the beginning of the week, an 82,000-dwt fixed from Kashima for a grains round voyage at $18,500, with a similar type fixed a few days later at $20,000, whilst larger types fixed coal from Australia with an 85,000-dwt fixed from Yeosu at $21,500 for a trip back to the Far East. The period market was active, albeit slightly tempered by the need for first employment, with a modern 82,000-dwt fixed for 2 years delivery China at $20,050 with the scrubber benefit shared between owners/charterers.

## Ultramax/Supramax

A week of consolidation with little movement or direction to the market. North America began the week looking softer, but as the week went on, rates remained relatively flat with a 63,000-dwt fixed from Altamira with petcoke to Bahudopi at $31,000 and a 61,000-dwt fixed from the Mississippi to East Mediterranean with coal at the same level. The Continent was steady in limited trading with a 61,000-dwt fixed at $21,500 for scrap from the Continent to East Mediterranean, but the Mediterranean market had a torrid week without much fresh demand and a lack of Black Sea grains. The South Atlantic benefited from a bounce in Panamax rates with a 64,000-dwt fixed from East Coast South America to the Far East at $19,850 plus $985,000 ballast bonus but was fairly unchanged over the course of the week. In Asia rates increased very slowly during the week with a 63,000-dwt fixed from South Korea for North Pacific grains to Southeast Asia at $21,000, as grain activity supported the market in the North, but further South Indonesia saw a lot more cargoes to India and Bangladesh which also drew tonnage from the Indian Ocean. South Africa looked flat with a 64,000-dwt agreeing $24,000 plus $240,000 ballast bonus from Port Elizabeth to China and the period market was more subdued with reported trades mostly concluded last week as charterers waited to see what direction the market would take.

Russian wheat loadings from the four deep-sea Black Sea terminals fell by around 60% during the five weeks to 28 August compared with the same period in 2025. (Figure 2 shows the underlying cargo volumes and voyage counts.) The reduction persisted throughout the period rather than reflecting a single disrupted week. Weekly volumes remained below the comparable 2025 range, with activity even lower during the second half of the window than at the beginning. Loadings were concentrated at Novorossiysk, as the port remained the principal outlet despite its own volume roughly halving. Vessel activity at Taman fell sharply, and no qualifying wheat loading was recorded at Kavkaz. Tuapse, the smallest of Russia’s deep-water grain terminals, remained in operation and was the only terminal to record an increase.

![Image 2](https://www.ajot.com/images/uploads/article/Signal_52_1.png)

Figure 2: Russian wheat loaded at Novorossiysk, Taman, Kavkaz and Tuapse over the matched load-date window 23 July–28 August, 2025 vs 2026. Upper panel measures cargo tonnage loaded, with the 2026 bar split between voyages that have completed and voyages still underway; lower-left panel counts vessel-voyages loaded, by class, with cargo carried to more than one discharge port counted as a single voyage; lower-right panel measures cargo tonnage loaded in each week of the window. The weekly panel covers the five full weeks to 26 August; the final two days of the window are included in all other figures (Source: Signal, Voyage Details).

Handysize remained the most active class but recorded a steep decline, while Supramax, Panamax and smaller-vessel employment also weakened. Handymax was the exception, registering slightly more voyages than a year earlier from a small base. The disruption has increased interest in alternative Baltic routes. Rail booking requests for grain bound for Russia’s Baltic terminals reached 5 million tonnes by 18 August, approaching the 6 million tonnes requested for Novorossiysk and Tuapse. Exporters are using Russian Baltic facilities, including Vysotsk, Ust-Luga, St Petersburg and Kaliningrad, while also considering transit through neighbouring Baltic states, particularly Latvia. The Baltic cannot fully replace the southern corridor. Russia’s Baltic terminals have an estimated annual grain-handling capacity of around 7 million tonnes, well below the volumes normally shipped through the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. Longer rail distances also add logistical complexity and raise export costs.

## MARKET OVERVIEW 

Diplomatic discussions between regional authorities have introduced a new framework for managing the Strait of Hormuz, outlining a roadmap toward a temporary navigational channel and coordinated mine-clearing initiatives. Under this structure, negotiators are evaluating a dual-lane transit corridor where vessels would enter the Persian Gulf through northern designated waters and exit via southern lanes, followed by further discussions to establish permanent operational and security arrangements. However, significant hurdles remain, particularly regarding demands to close the existing southern route along the Omani coastline and potential methods for maritime service administration. With stakeholders continuing to reject any framework that imposes passage conditions or compromises absolute freedom of navigation, fleet operators remain cautious about an immediate, unencumbered return to the waterway. Despite the persistent threat, crude outflows from the Persian Gulf have quietly rebounded as regional producers utilise shuttle networks to move shut-in volumes onto the global market. Daily volumes passing out of the region have climbed back toward an estimated 6~8 million barrels, supported by major loading surges across key export facilities in Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia. To circumvent security risks, producers are increasingly relying on dedicated shuttle tankers to transport crude just beyond the strait, where cargoes are transferred to awaiting international carriers anchored off coastal bunkering hubs. This revival of seaborne flows has exerted downward pressure on international crude benchmarks, driving futures back toward US$88 a barrel and delivering the sharpest weekly price softening in two months. This model has created unprecedented profitability for tanker operators willing to navigate the high-risk zone, with freight earnings for VLCCs touching historic highs. Energy majors and trading houses are capitalising on significant price discounts on inland barrels, absorbing elevated shipping costs that equate to roughly US$10 per barrel to deliver cargoes to worldwide refining hubs. However, the market remains sharply bifurcated; while crude supply chains are gradually adapting and softening prompt oil benchmarks, refined product markets continue to face severe tightness. 

With substantial regional refining capacity still offline and international processing assets facing overseas disruptions, downstream fuel segments like diesel and gasoline are seeing sustained upward margin pressure, highlighting an uneven recovery across the global maritime trade. Dry Bulk Rates Ride Rising Trade 

The dry bulk freight market delivered a considerably stronger performance during the first seven months of 2026, with Baltic Exchange time -charter equivalent earn-ings improving across all four major vessel segments com-pared with January–July 2025. The recovery was broad -

based rather than dependent on a single vessel class, re-flecting stronger cargo volumes, improved fleet utilisation and firmer demand across both major and minor bulk trades. Based on the available daily assessments, the Capesize 5TC averaged approximately USD 30,400/day, up 81% from USD 16,800/day during the corresponding period of 2025. Capesize earnings reached a high of USD 46,538/day in late May, while the market closed July at USD 35,457/day, well above the USD 26,858/day recorded at the end of July last year. The improvement extended across the smaller segments. Kamsarmax earnings averaged around USD 17,600/day, increasing 53% year -on -year from USD 11,500/day, while the Ultramax 11TC rose by 48% also near to USD 17,600/day. Handysize earnings recorded the smallest, but still substantial, increase, averaging USD 14,100/day compared with USD 10,100/day in 2025, representing growth of 39%. The progression of rates was also important. Following a relatively stable opening quarter, earnings strengthened sharply during April and May, particu-larly for Capesizes and Kamsarmaxes. Ultramax and Handysize markets advanced more steadily, reaching their strong-est levels during June and July and demonstrating healthier underlying support across geographically diversified trades. This stronger freight environment was accompanied by an increase in total seaborne dry bulk volumes. Based on the Signal Ocean data, approximately 3.41 billion tonnes were transported during January–July 2026, compared with 3.35 billion tonnes during the same period of 2025, representing growth of almost 2%. Capesize -carried cargo increased by 4.8% to 936.7 million tonnes, lifting its share of total trade from 26.7% to 27.4%. Panamax, Supramax and Handymax volumes also increased, while VLOC, Handysize and Small vessel cargoes declined. The figures therefore indicate that trade growth was concentrated mainly in the larger and medium -sized vessel categories, supporting the segments that experienced the strongest freight improvement. Commodity flows remained dominated by iron ore and coal, which together represented more than 52% of total dry bulk trade. Iron ore volumes increased by 1.5% to 992.2 million tonnes, while coal shipments rose by 2.1% to 788.9 million tonnes. Grain trade delivered a more pro-nounced increase of 10.4%, reaching 358.9 million tonnes and overtaking other ores and rocks as the third -

largest cargo category. By contrast, fertilizers, steel, ce-ment and forestry products declined, confirming that 

overall growth was driven primarily by the traditional 

core commodities. Australia remained the largest origin, increasing exports to 844.8 million tonnes, followed by Brazil at 374.1 million tonnes. Guinea recorded one of the strongest increases, rising 22% to 131.9 million tonnes, supporting long -haul bauxite movements. China remained overwhelmingly the largest destination, receiv-ing 1.36 billion tonnes, up 2.9% year -on -year and repre-senting almost 40% of global dry bulk imports. South Korea, Vietnam and Indonesia also increased intake, while India declined by almost 5%. Overall, the 2026 freight recovery appears firmly connected to improving physical trade. Higher iron ore, coal and grain volumes, combined with stronger long -haul exports from Australia, Brazil and Guinea, in-creased vessel employment and supported rates across the market. # Week 35 | Tuesday 01st September 2026 Market Insight 

By  Nikos Tagoulis, Senior Analyst 

The EUA market maintained its upward trend in August, despite the quieter trading conditions and lower liquidity that typically characterize the holiday period. The advance extended the recov-ery that began in late March and left the EU ETS on a constructive footing heading into autumn. The Front Dec -26 EUA contract av-eraged €82.36 /ton during August and at the time of writing read €83.30 /ton, around 6.5% above the 2026 y -t-d average. Prices remained within a relatively narrow range during the month, and the contract continued to trade above its 50 -, 100 - and 200 -day moving averages. 

The European gas market has contributed to the firming of EUAs. Prices at the Dutch TTF hub rose significantly as geopolitical ten-sions leading to Qatari volumes off market, low European storage levels and competition from Asian buyers for LNG cargoes height-ened concerns over winter supply. 

Although the correlation between front -month TTF gas prices and 

EUAs fluctuated in August, it has strengthened recently, suggest-ing that prevailing gas -market dynamics are supporting EUA de-mand. The principal transmission channel is fuel -switching eco-nomics: higher gas prices make coal more competitive with gas for power generation, encouraging more carbon -intensive output and increasing utilities ’ demand for allowances. 

Furthermore, recent economic signals add to this supportive backdrop, pointing to firm industrial demand. The August euro-

zone manufacturing PMI reached its strongest level in more than 

four years, accompanied by stronger new orders, a recovery in exports and the first increase in factory employment after more than three years. Together, these developments strengthen the outlook for EUA demand. 

Despite the positive backdrop, traders remain cautious. Invest-ment funds have reduced their net -long exposure in recent weeks, while commercial participants have continued to increase their forward exposure, reflecting hedging strategies built around expectations of further EUA price increases. The divergence indi-cates that commercial buying remains driven by risk management even as speculative interest weakens. Compliance buying adds another source of demand ahead of September 30, including from shipping companies as the maritime sector ’s obligations continue to phase in. In 2026, shipping companies must surrender allow-ances covering 70% of their verified 2025 emissions within the scope of the EU ETS, rising to 100% of 2026 emissions in the fol-lowing year, with higher EUA prices increasing the compliance cost of voyages covered by the scheme. 

Looking ahead, policy is re -emerging as a major driver. The Com-

mission ’s July proposal for the post -2030 EU ETS would slow the contraction of the emissions cap, extend conditional free alloca-tion and ease the operation of the Market Stability Reserve. The measures would leave more allowances in circulation than under the present framework, easing concerns about future supply con-straints. The initial market response was positive, however, this is only the starting point for further negotiations, leaving scope for revision. 

Beyond the EU ETS reform, the proposed linkage with the UK ETS 

remains an open issue. A summit expected to advance negotia-tions in July was postponed following the change in UK leader-ship, leaving the timetable uncertain. Progress towards linkage should narrow the spread between UKAs and EUAs as UK allow-ance prices move closer to EU levels. Once implemented, the link-age could become a bearish factor for EUA prices by expanding the pool of available allowances, although its impact would de-pend on supply conditions across both systems. 

Concluding, the EUA outlook for the remainder of 2026 will de-

pend largely on developments across the European energy com-plex. Geopolitical uncertainty, disruption to Middle Eastern LNG flows and Europe ’s efforts to replenish low gas storage levels will shape gas and power prices, with changes in fuel -switching eco-nomics feeding through to carbon. In the near term, compliance buying, improving industrial activity and commercial hedging should underpin EUA prices, while progress on EU ETS reform and EU–UK linkage will shape the longer -term direction. www.intermodal.gr 

2

Crude tanker spot markets eased overall this week, with Su-ezmaxes suffering the largest losses while VLCCs posted modest gains. The BDTI averaged 2,855, down 3% w -o-w. 

Within the VLCC segment, regional performance was mixed. The 

Middle East market remained stable, supported by the growing use of AIS -dark transits through Hormuz, followed by STS trans-fers off Fujairah or Sohar. Conditions stayed healthy, with steady enquiry and balanced tonnage availability. West Africa spot rates retreated w -o-w despite limited tonnage, as demand faded pro-gressively through the week. The US Gulf opened firmly, carrying forward the previous week ’s momentum, but a series of failed fixtures pulled rates lower and weighed on sentiment. Meanwhile, owners sought longer -period employment for their tonnage. VLCC TCE rates averaged $334,066/day, up 3% w -o-w. 

The expected retreat following the elevated rates of previous 

weeks materialized for Suezmaxes, shifting negotiating power towards charterers. Rates corrected sharply in the Americas, Black Sea and West Africa as demand and fixing activity weak-ened, leaving ample tonnage chasing limited cargoes. In the Black Sea, some owners avoided the region in search of safer and more economically attractive employment, while at USG, Suezmaxes lost cargoes to more competitive Aframaxes. Markdown Content:
Week 35 tracks 164 freight assessments across six shipping sectors with a three-week AI outlook. Gulf tanker markets remain elevated but increasingly route-specific, East-of-Suez CPP stays firm, dry bulk has strengthened prompt, while gas and container markets continue to show a clear split between spot and period signals.

**Freight Market Outlook - Week 35 (2026)**

**Published: 31 August 2026**

**Current market observation: 28 August 2026**

**Three-week forecast horizon: 4–18 September 2026**

Week 35 brings another **164-route cross-sector view**, but the key message this week is not simply whether freight is rising or falling.

It is **where the strength sits, how long it may last, and which routes are already moving differently from their wider sector**.

That divergence is especially clear in tankers, while dry bulk has strengthened in the prompt market and gas continues to show a sizeable gap between spot and period employment.

**Crude & DPP Tankers: strong market, but route selection is everything**

Hormuz disruption continues to keep Gulf risk elevated, but Week 35 tanker performance is increasingly split. **MEG–Asia VLCC trades remain very strong**, while Atlantic VLCC and several Suezmax routes have corrected.

The report’s expert note therefore puts greater emphasis on vessel positioning and route selection than on headline tanker strength alone.

The numbers illustrate that difference. The c.2010-built **VLCC Average TCE** is around **$221,000/day**, with the model moving to roughly **$234,000/day, $295,000/day and $288,000/day** over the forward window. Meanwhile,

Suezmax average earnings have corrected to about **$165,000/day**, but recover progressively toward approximately **$227,000/day by Week +3**.

The clearest forward signal, however, is **Aframax**. Average TCE has dropped to around **$86,000/day**, but the model rebuilds earnings toward **$123,000/day by Week +3**.

TD25 shows a similar recovery pattern.

**Shipbroker view:** tanker freight remains highly rewarding, but fixing strategy matters. Owners should not assume every crude route will follow the Gulf headline higher; charterers, meanwhile, may find the better opportunities on routes where the prompt correction has run ahead of the wider fundamentals.

**Product & CPP Tankers: firm East of Suez, recovery opportunities in the Atlantic**

CPP remains highly regional. East-of-Suez LR demand is stronger than Atlantic MR prompt markets, with changing Asia-to-Africa diesel flows adding support to long-haul clean-product employment.

**TC1 ME Gulf–Japan** is currently around **WS 541** and moves higher initially before easing later. **TC5 ME–Japan** is even stronger near **WS 577**, with the model showing further near-term upside before some normalisation in the outer week.

The Atlantic offers a different opportunity. **Rotterdam–New York**, **Augusta–Lavera** and **Houston–Amsterdam** are softer prompt, but their forecast curves show meaningful recovery potential later in the window.

**Shipbroker view:** this is not a market to trade from an average CPP headline. Owners need to distinguish between prompt Atlantic weakness and stronger eastern fundamentals; charterers should equally recognise that some currently soft Atlantic routes may become more expensive if the forecast recovery develops.

**Chemical & Vegetable Oils: supported, but not a breakout**

Palm-oil demand remains supported by Indian festival buying, while Malaysian exports have been healthy. At the same time, higher production and inventories keep physical supply comfortable and limit the case for a sustained freight rally.

**Port Kelang–Rotterdam** holds around **$30,000/day**, firms marginally in Week +1, then eases toward approximately **$28,200/day by Week +3**.

The route therefore remains workable, but the forward profile favours disciplined fixing rather than chasing the prompt market.

**Gas Carriers: period cover remains the stronger story**

Gas shipping continues to show a pronounced **spot-versus-period split**. LNG spot remains weak, LPG spot has softened, while longer-duration VLGC and LPG employment is considerably more resilient.

The **160k CBM LNG spot rate** is only around **$16,250/day**, while the smaller 145k CBM benchmark remains around **$4,500/day**. By contrast, the **84k CBM VLGC one-year TC** holds near **$70,000/day** throughout the forecast horizon.

BLPG3 Houston–Chiba has eased to around **$267/tonne**, while Ras Tanura–Chiba VLGC TCE briefly firms before softening later.

**Shipbroker view:** prompt gas employment still carries more downside and volatility than period cover. Owners able to secure quality duration have a more defensible earnings profile than those relying solely on the spot cycle.

Markdown Content:
Week 35 tracks 164 freight assessments across six shipping sectors with a three-week AI outlook. Gulf tanker markets remain elevated but increasingly route-specific, East-of-Suez CPP stays firm, dry bulk has strengthened prompt, while gas and container markets continue to show a clear split between spot and period signals.

**Freight Market Outlook - Week 35 (2026)**

**Published: 31 August 2026**

**Current market observation: 28 August 2026**

**Three-week forecast horizon: 4–18 September 2026**

Week 35 brings another **164-route cross-sector view**, but the key message this week is not simply whether freight is rising or falling.

It is **where the strength sits, how long it may last, and which routes are already moving differently from their wider sector**.

That divergence is especially clear in tankers, while dry bulk has strengthened in the prompt market and gas continues to show a sizeable gap between spot and period employment.

**Crude & DPP Tankers: strong market, but route selection is everything**

Hormuz disruption continues to keep Gulf risk elevated, but Week 35 tanker performance is increasingly split. **MEG–Asia VLCC trades remain very strong**, while Atlantic VLCC and several Suezmax routes have corrected.

The report’s expert note therefore puts greater emphasis on vessel positioning and route selection than on headline tanker strength alone.

The numbers illustrate that difference. The c.2010-built **VLCC Average TCE** is around **$221,000/day**, with the model moving to roughly **$234,000/day, $295,000/day and $288,000/day** over the forward window. Meanwhile,

Suezmax average earnings have corrected to about **$165,000/day**, but recover progressively toward approximately **$227,000/day by Week +3**.

The clearest forward signal, however, is **Aframax**. Average TCE has dropped to around **$86,000/day**, but the model rebuilds earnings toward **$123,000/day by Week +3**.

TD25 shows a similar recovery pattern.

**Shipbroker view:** tanker freight remains highly rewarding, but fixing strategy matters. Owners should not assume every crude route will follow the Gulf headline higher; charterers, meanwhile, may find the better opportunities on routes where the prompt correction has run ahead of the wider fundamentals.

**Product & CPP Tankers: firm East of Suez, recovery opportunities in the Atlantic**

CPP remains highly regional. East-of-Suez LR demand is stronger than Atlantic MR prompt markets, with changing Asia-to-Africa diesel flows adding support to long-haul clean-product employment.

**TC1 ME Gulf–Japan** is currently around **WS 541** and moves higher initially before easing later. **TC5 ME–Japan** is even stronger near **WS 577**, with the model showing further near-term upside before some normalisation in the outer week.

The Atlantic offers a different opportunity. **Rotterdam–New York**, **Augusta–Lavera** and **Houston–Amsterdam** are softer prompt, but their forecast curves show meaningful recovery potential later in the window.

**Shipbroker view:** this is not a market to trade from an average CPP headline. Owners need to distinguish between prompt Atlantic weakness and stronger eastern fundamentals; charterers should equally recognise that some currently soft Atlantic routes may become more expensive if the forecast recovery develops.

**Chemical & Vegetable Oils: supported, but not a breakout**

Palm-oil demand remains supported by Indian festival buying, while Malaysian exports have been healthy. At the same time, higher production and inventories keep physical supply comfortable and limit the case for a sustained freight rally.

**Port Kelang–Rotterdam** holds around **$30,000/day**, firms marginally in Week +1, then eases toward approximately **$28,200/day by Week +3**.

The route therefore remains workable, but the forward profile favours disciplined fixing rather than chasing the prompt market.

**Gas Carriers: period cover remains the stronger story**

Gas shipping continues to show a pronounced **spot-versus-period split**. LNG spot remains weak, LPG spot has softened, while longer-duration VLGC and LPG employment is considerably more resilient.

The **160k CBM LNG spot rate** is only around **$16,250/day**, while the smaller 145k CBM benchmark remains around **$4,500/day**. By contrast, the **84k CBM VLGC one-year TC** holds near **$70,000/day** throughout the forecast horizon.

BLPG3 Houston–Chiba has eased to around **$267/tonne**, while Ras Tanura–Chiba VLGC TCE briefly firms before softening later.

**Shipbroker view:** prompt gas employment still carries more downside and volatility than period cover. Owners able to secure quality duration have a more defensible earnings profile than those relying solely on the spot cycle.

**Dry Bulk: prompt strength is real, but the forward curve is more cautious**

Dry bulk strengthened materially in Week 35, led by **Capesize and a broad Panamax–Kamsarmax rebound**. Atlantic Capesize demand and tighter tonnage helped lift prompt earnings sharply.

The **Average Capesize TCE** has risen to around **$45,200/day**, but the SSB curve moderates toward approximately **$33,900/day by Week +3**. Panamax earnings also firm prompt, while the forward curve becomes softer later.

Supramax is steadier, with average earnings near **$23,400/day**, while selected Atlantic Handysize routes retain better forward support.

**Shipbroker view:** owners have good reason to defend current prompt levels, particularly in Capesize, but the forward curve argues against assuming today’s strength automatically rolls into late September.

**Container: the lane matters more than the index**

Container markets remain highly lane-specific. US West Coast spot freight has firmed slightly, Europe has softened, and US East Coast remains comparatively stable. Meanwhile, vessel time-charter values barely move.

The **SCFI Comprehensive Index** stands near **3,510**, with the model easing toward **3,302** in Week +1 before a partial recovery. Shanghai–Europe also weakens first and then recovers, while the **2,750 TEU time-charter benchmark remains close to $41,800/day** throughout the window.

For commercial teams, the conclusion is straightforward: **trade-lane capacity and positioning matter more than a single container headline index**.

**Week 35 Commercial View**

Across the six sectors:

*   **Crude/DPP:** still strong, but Aframax provides the clearest recovery signal while Suezmax remains more selective.
*   **CPP:** East of Suez remains firm; selected Atlantic MR routes offer later recovery potential.
*   **Chemical/Vegetable Oils:** supported near term, but supply prevents a convincing breakout.
*   **Gas:** period employment continues to outperform a weaker spot environment.
*   **Dry Bulk:** prompt strength is constructive, but the outer curve is more restrained.
*   **Container:** spot markets diverge by lane while vessel TC values remain remarkably stable.

Week 35 is therefore a market of **divergence rather than uniform direction**. The commercial edge lies in identifying where the forward curve differs from today’s headline rate and positioning before that gap closes.

Markdown Content:
Black Sea Summer Slump 

Dry bulk trade from the Black Sea has moved into a mark-edly weaker phase during the summer months, with ex-ports from Russia and Ukraine falling sharply compared with the preceding spring period. Based on Signal Ocean data, between June and August 2026, combined dry bulk shipments reached 21.60 million MT, down 42.0% from the 37.27 million MT exported during March–May. Cargo departures followed the same direction, declining from 2,323 to 1,302 voyages, a 43.9% contraction. Although part of this fall reflects the normal transition between agricultural seasons, the magnitude of the decline in-creasingly points to geopolitical and operational disrup-tion rather than seasonality alone. 

June was clearly the strongest month of the summer, with Russia and Ukraine shipping a combined 11.46 million MT across 683 cargoes. Russia accounted for 7.07 million MT and Ukraine for 4.39 million MT, supported by remaining old -

crop agricultural volumes and relatively steady mineral flows. In July, however, activity weakened considerably. Com-bined exports fell to 8.01 million MT, 30.1% below June, with Russian volumes declining to 5.38 million MT and Ukrain-ian shipments to 2.63 million MT. The usual pre -harvest lull played a role, but deteriorating security conditions also 

began to affect vessel availability, port operations and chartering appetite. 

The deterioration became significantly more visible in August. As of August 26, combined recorded loadings stand at only 2.13 million MT, comprising 1.76 million MT from Russia and just 0.37 million MT from Ukraine. These figures re-main incomplete and should improve as month -end operations are recorded, yet the current gap is too large to be ex-plained purely by timing. Since July, attacks on port facilities, terminals and commercial vessels have intensified across the region. Ukrainian deepwater ports have operated under severe pressure, while Russian grain terminals around Novorossiysk and navigation through parts of the Azov -Black Sea system have also faced disruption. Market reports indicate that these attacks have delayed cargoes, restricted export capacity and made owners increasingly reluctant to commit tonnage without substantially higher freight and war -risk compensation. 

The three -month comparison highlights that Ukraine has absorbed the heavier impact. Russian Black Sea dry bulk ex-ports declined 37.6%, from 22.79 million MT in March– May to 14.21 million MT during June–August, while Ukrainian exports fell 49.0%, from 14.48 million MT to 

7.39 million MT. Russia consequently increased its share 

of combined exports from 61.1% to 65.8%. Yet this should not necessarily be interpreted as Russian strength; rather, Russian flows have simply proved more resilient than Ukrainian ones. For the dry bulk market, the implications extend beyond lost tonnes. Lower Black Sea volumes reduce employment opportunities for Handysize, Supramax and Panamax tonnage traditionally active in regional grain and minor -bulk trades, while higher insurance premiums and security risks discourage owners from fixing into the area. At the same time, any redirection of grain toward alternative suppliers such as North or South America could partially compensate through longer tonne -miles. Therefore, the Black Sea is currently offering less cargo, but potentially more distance elsewhere—a trade -off that could become increasingly important for dry bulk utilisation if the disruption persists into the autumn export season. 

IN A NUTSHELL: 

• Black Sea dry bulk exports fell 42% versus the preceding spring period. (Page 1) 

• Ukraine suffered the sharper contraction, with summer ex-ports declining by 49%. (Page 1) 

• August loadings weakened dramatically as security risks 

> disrupted regional shipping operations. (Page 1)

• Lower regional cargoes pressure vessel demand despite po-tential tonne -mile trade substitution. (Page 1) 

• Crude oil fell to $83.4 a barrel on Friday, extending weekly losses to about 4%. (Page 8)

See the report for sources and charts.
